title: Product Development: Three Routes From Idea to Production | BOOM Drinkware
description: Customize an existing model, change one component, or develop a new product from a drawing. What each route costs, what drives the timeline, and the six steps from concept review to mass production.

blocks.h1: From a Sketch, a Sample or Nothing at All
blocks.lead: Most projects arrive as a photo of something close, with a list of what is wrong with it. That is enough to start. The first question is never “what do you want to make” — it is “how far from what already exists do you need to be”.
blocks.image_alt: Development and sample work at the Baoyuanfeng factory
blocks.caption: Development work stays with the team that will mould the part — not a separate design office.

blocks.intro: The route decides the cost, the minimum order and how long the project takes. Choosing the smallest route that solves the problem is usually the difference between a product that ships this season and one that does not.

items.title: 01 · Customize an existing product
items.text: Take a model from the library and change what the buyer sees: colour, finish, print, laser mark, lid option, packing. No tooling, fastest route, 10 pieces on eligible configurations.

items.title: 02 · Modify one component
items.text: Keep the body, change the part that makes it yours — a new lid, a different rim, an insert, a base. One small mould instead of a product's worth of tooling, and the body stays on an existing tool.

items.title: 03 · Develop a new product
items.text: A structure that does not exist yet: new body, new lid, new proportions. 2–4 mould sets, DFM review, trial rounds, then a 10,000 piece production minimum to carry the tooling.

blocks.text: If your design can be delivered by route 01 or 02, we will say so — even when route 03 is the more profitable answer for us. A mould cut for a product that did not need one is a customer lost at the second order.

blocks.h2: Four things, and only one of them is the design fee.
blocks.intro: Development cost is mostly tooling and trial time, not drawing time. This is what to expect before you approve a route.

blocks.h2: Six steps from brief to mass production.
blocks.intro: Every step ends with something written down. The point is not bureaucracy — it is that a change after T1 costs tooling time, while the same change before T1 costs an email.

items.title: Brief and concept review
items.text: What the product has to do, who uses it, the market it sells into, the target quantity and price. Reference photos are welcome; a competitor sample is even better.

items.title: Route and DFM
items.text: We say which of the three routes fits, and what will be difficult in the drawing: thin sections, undercuts, threads, tolerance between lid and body.

items.title: Drawing or 3D model
items.text: We work from your file, or produce one from the brief. Rendered views and a dimensioned drawing come back for approval before any steel is cut.

items.title: Tooling and T1
items.text: The mould is cut, fitted and trialled. T1 parts are measured against the drawing, assembled and sent to you with the measurements.

items.title: Sample approval
items.text: T2 or T3 corrects what T1 showed. The approved sample — with artwork version and dimension sheet — becomes the standard for production.

items.title: Mass production
items.text: Production runs on the approved tool at the agreed MOQ, 25–30 days to ship, with first-off parts retained as the reference.

blocks.h2: What makes a development enquiry answerable.
blocks.intro: None of these are gates. But an enquiry with all six gets a route recommendation and a cost shape in the first reply, instead of three emails of clarification.

items.title: The job the product does
items.text: Cold drink, hot drink, single serve, resale, giveaway. It decides wall thickness, material and lid type more than aesthetics do.

items.title: A reference
items.text: A product you like, a product you dislike, or your own sketch. Anything visual shortens the first exchange.

items.title: Volume and price target
items.text: First order and annual repeat, plus the unit price you need to hit. It tells us whether route 01 is even viable.

items.title: Material constraints
items.text: Food contact, recyclability, BPA-free, hot-fill, dishwasher — each one eliminates some options immediately.

items.title: Decoration intent
items.text: Print, laser, label, or bare. A part designed for a full wrap print is moulded differently from one that stays blank.

items.title: Market and documents
items.text: Destination country and the compliance documents your buyer will ask for, so testing is planned rather than discovered.

items: Can you develop a product from a photo only?

We can start from a photo, and we will tell you what cannot be inferred from it: internal dimensions, wall thickness, material and thread geometry. Those come from a sample, a drawing, or a first round of tooling with iteration.
Yes, on request, before drawings are exchanged. Send yours or ask for ours.
You do, on a development project paid by you. We do not resell a customer's proprietary shape — and we say that in writing rather than in a sales conversation.
What if the product needs a component we do not make?
We say which parts are outside our process — metal bodies, glass, electronic modules — and quote them as sourced items with the source stated. We do not pass a sourced part off as our own moulding.
